questions.subject: network-theory
questions.question: A voltage drop across a non-linear element is given by \(v=i+2i^2\). The power loss across it for a current of \(\sin t\) is
questions.explanation: Given, \[i(t)=\sin t \tag{i}\] \[v=i+2i^2 \tag{ii}\] From (i) and (ii), \[v(t)=\sin t+2\sin^2 t\] The instantaneous power consumed is \[p(t)=v(t)i(t)\] \[p(t)=\left(\sin t+2\sin^2 t\right)\sin t\] \[p(t)=\sin^2 t+2\sin^3 t\] Using \[\sin^2 t=\frac{1-\cos 2t}{2}, \qquad \sin^3 t=\frac{3\sin t-\sin 3t}{4}\] \[p(t) = \frac{1-\cos 2t}{2} + \frac{3\sin t-\sin 3t}{2}\] \[p(t) = \frac{1}{2} +\frac{3}{2}\sin t -\frac{1}{2}\cos 2t -\frac{1}{2}\sin 3t\] The average power is the DC component: \[P_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{1}{2}=0.5\,\text{W}\] \[\boxed{\text{D) 0.5 W}}\]

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question: A linear phase low-pass filter with a cut-off frequency of \(1500~\text{Hz}\) shifts a \(50~\text{Hz}\) signal by \(3~\text{ms}\). It will shift a signal of \(150~\text{Hz}\) by
questions.explanation:
Given A linear phase low-pass filter shifts a \(50~\text{Hz}\) signal by \(3~\text{ms}.\) A linear phase filter has a constant group delay over its passband. Hence, every frequency component within the passband experiences the same time delay. Since both \(50~\text{Hz}\) and \(150~\text{Hz}\) lie within the passband (\(f_c=1500~\text{Hz}\)),\[\boxed{\text{Delay at }150~\text{Hz}=3~\text{ms}.}\]Therefore,\[\boxed{\text{(A) }3~\text{ms}}\]
Key points
  • A linear phase filter provides constant group delay.
  • All frequency components within the passband experience the same time delay.
  • Group delay is independent of frequency for an ideal linear phase filter.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not assume the delay is proportional to frequency.
  • Do not confuse phase delay with group delay.

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: The differential input resistance of the circuit shown in figure is
questions.explanation: The differential input resistance is defined as \[R_{in}=\frac{V_{i}}{I_{i}}\] Since the op-amp input currents are ideally zero, the differential input current \(I_{i}\) flows through the two resistors \(R_{1}\) connected to the input terminals. Applying KVL, \[V_{i}=I_{i}R_{1}+I_{i}R_{1}\] \[V_{i}=2I_{i}R_{1}\] Hence, \[R_{in}=\frac{V_{i}}{I_{i}}=2R_{1}\] \[\boxed{\text{(c) }2R_{1}}\]

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: In the circuit shown in figure, if \(e_{\text{i}} = \sin t\), the voltage \(V_0\) is
questions.explanation: The op-amp is configured as a non-inverting amplifier. Its closed-loop gain is \[A_{v}=1+\frac{R_{f}}{R_{1}} =1+\frac{10\,\text{k}\Omega}{10\,\text{k}\Omega} =2\] The input network is an RC low-pass filter with \[R=100\,\text{k}\Omega,\qquad C=10\,\mu\text{F}\] Hence, \[RC=100\times10^{3}\times10\times10^{-6}=1\,\text{s}\] For \[e_{i}=\sin t,\qquad \omega=1\,\text{rad/s}\] the transfer function of the RC network is \[H(j\omega)=\frac{1}{1+j\omega RC} =\frac{1}{1+j}\] Therefore, \[|H|=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},\qquad \angle H=-\frac{\pi}{4}\] Thus, the voltage at the non-inverting input is \[V_{+}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \sin\!\left(t-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\] The output is \[V_{o}=2V_{+} =2\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \sin\!\left(t-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\] \[V_{o}=\sqrt{2}\, \sin\!\left(t-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\] \[\boxed{\text{(a) }\sqrt{2}\sin\!\left(t-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)}\]

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.question: An 8 bit ADC outputs all 1s when \(V_{in}\) = 1.275 V. The quantization error is
questions.explanation:
Given:
  • \(V_{FS}\) = 1.275 V
  • \(n\) = 8
\[\text{Step size } \Delta = \frac{V_{max} - V_{min}}{2^n-1} = \frac{1.275}{2^8-1}\] \[\text{Quantization error = }\pm \frac{\Delta}{2} = \pm \frac{1.275}{2(2^8-1)} = \pm \; 2.5 \text{ mV}\] \[\boxed{(D) \; \pm \; 2.5 \text{ mV} }\]

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question:
Match the roots in the \(s\)-plane with the impulse response shown in figure Column I : Impulse Response Column II : Roots in the \(s\)-plane A. Two imaginary Roots
B. Two complex roots in the left half plane
C. A single root on the negative real axis
D. A single root at the origin
questions.explanation:
The correct matching between roots in the \(s\)-plane and their impulse response is determined below:
  • (a) Two imaginary roots: Roots lie at \(s = \pm j\omega\). The response is purely sinusoidal with constant amplitude \(\implies\) (ii).
  • (b) Two complex roots in the left half plane: Roots lie at \(s = -\sigma \pm j\omega_d\). The response is an exponentially decaying sinusoid \(\implies\) (iii).
  • (c) A single root on the negative real axis: Root lies at \(s = -\alpha\). The response is a purely decaying exponential curve \(\implies\) (i).
  • (d) A single root at the origin: Root lies at \(s = 0\). The transfer function is \(1/s\), and the impulse response is a step function (constant magnitude) \(\implies\) (iv).
\[\boxed{\text{(a)-(ii), (b)-(iii), (c)-(i), (d)-(iv)}}\]
Key points

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question: Which of the following transfer functions has a minimum phase characteristic?
questions.explanation:
A minimum phase system has all its poles and zeros in the left half of the \(s\)-plane and does not contain a time delay.
  • (A) \(\displaystyle \frac{1+s}{1-s}\) has a pole at \(s=1\) (RHP) \(\Rightarrow\) Not minimum phase.
  • (B) \(\displaystyle \frac{1-s}{1+s}\) has a zero at \(s=1\) (RHP) \(\Rightarrow\) Not minimum phase.
  • (C) \(\displaystyle \frac{e^{-3s}}{s}\) contains a time delay \(e^{-3s}\), which introduces additional phase lag \(\Rightarrow\) Not minimum phase.
  • (D) \(\displaystyle \frac{s}{(s+1)(s+2)}\) has poles at \(s=-1,-2\) and a zero at \(s=0\). There are no right-half-plane poles or zeros and no time delay. Hence, it is a minimum phase system.
\[\boxed{(D)\;\dfrac{s}{(s+1)(s+2)}}\]
